newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Unrest reaches Tirana, airport closed.
newsitem.headline: Unrest reaches Tirana, airport closed.

text.p: Albania's armed revolt crept closer to Tirana on Thursday as residents woke to find the capital's military academy had been looted of weapons during the night.
In further signs that the small Balkan country is sliding towards anarchy, doctors reported five people had died in the northern city of Shkoder as looters seized arms from army depots.
International airline officials reported that Tirana airport was closed, hampering the evacuation of some foreign embassy staff and families ordered by their governments.
A European mediation mission headed by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky had been due to fly to Tirana on Thursday to resume its efforts to halt the unrest.
On Wednesday, a Greek airliner aborted a landing at Tirana because the airport was closed. A foreign ministry spokesman in Athens said shooting was heard.
The new developments came only a few hours after Albania's new prime minister Bashkim Fino announced an all-party government that he hopes can restore order and appealed for calm and reconciliation.

Looters raided the military academy in the east of the capital during the night and seized an unknown quantity of weapons, leaving uniforms and boxes scattered outside, according to residents. The building was deserted on Thursday morning.
Another barracks in the Tirana outer suburb of Kombinat was also raided on Wednesday evening, residents said.

For the first time since unrest sparked by anger of failed savings schemes erupted in the south of the country last month, shooting could be clearly heard in Tirana as newly-acquired weapons were fired in celebration.

Residents in Shkoder, previously untouched by the unrest, reported that civilians had looted a tank unit at Mergusha, five km (three miles) from the city, along with the main army barracks in the city centre.
Doctors in Shkoder hospital said five people had died and several people had been wounded during the looting.
Albania's "government of national reconciliation", its 15 ministries divided among nine parties, was to be sworn in on Thursday, its main aim to stage new elections by June.

Prime Minister Fino, a Socialist from Gjirokaster, one of the southern towns now in rebel hands, said on Wednesday evening: "After consultations with all political forces we have tried to make a government for all Albanians."
"I call on Albanians in these times to think about Albania, not political forces."
Bashkim says he wants dialogue with rebels in the south who continue to insist right-wing President Ali Berisha resign before they hand in thousands of weapons seized from depots.

The rebels accuse Berisha of allowing pyramid savings schemes to flourish. Most of the schemes collapsed earlier this year, wiping out the life savings of thousands of families, particularly in the more prosperous south of the country.

In some parts of the south the rebellion in which more than 40 people have died has visibly deteriorated into lawlessness. Armed gangs roamed at will through rebel-held towns, robbing motorists, terrorising women, shooting at travellers from Greece and ignoring warnings of stern punishment issued by insurgent "defence councils".
The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday it was ordering 160 government employees and their dependents to leave by regular or charter flights. Another 2,000 Americans were urged to go.
A diplomatic source said orders this week by most Western countries to pull out stemmed from "logical safety criteria. They have no reflection on the country or the government".
U.S. ambassador Marisa Lino appeared on the Wednesdsay evening news urging viewers to back the new government. "You cannot build a democracy by resorting to violence," she said in Albanian.
